segments.name: Huntington, and the Colleges of the Middle West

stops.name: Huntington, Indiana: the ninth surviving child
stops.date_confidence: attested (Wikipedia, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman'; Huntington County Honors). The coordinate is Huntington town center: the family's farm site is not independently located in anything reached, and no source consulted gives an address. The mother's name is Sophia Strock Smith; the pool's geography lens carried a misspelling, 'Sopha Strock', corrected here.
stops.campa: On farm ground near Huntington, Indiana, John Marion Smith, a Quaker dairy farmer who also keeps a bank, and his wife Sophia Strock have their ninth surviving child on the twenty-sixth of August, and they name her Elizebeth. The exact house does not survive in the record, and the town is as close as the documents come. Nothing else about her first eighteen years is set down in any source reached: no schooling, no illness, no move. She is the last of nine in a Quaker farming household, born to a father who runs a dairy herd and a bank at once.
suggested_refs: The Indiana state historical marker at Huntington, dedicated August 2021

stops.name: The University of Wooster, Ohio: four languages and an interrupted degree
stops.date_confidence: attested for 1911 to 1913 (Wikipedia, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman'); month and day default to 09-01. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 40.8081/-81.9346, roughly 400 m off campus, to the College of Wooster infobox value 40.81167/-81.935494. Note the institution was named the University of Wooster during her years there; the College of Wooster name dates from 1915.
stops.campa: At nineteen she enters the University of Wooster in Ohio, which will not take the name College of Wooster until 1915, and reads English, Greek, Latin, and German. Greek and Latin are construed rather than read. The daily exercise is holding a system of forms in the head and testing an unknown string against it until the string parses or fails to, which is also, though nobody at Wooster has a name for it, what cryptanalysis will ask of her. Two years in, her mother falls ill, and she leaves without a degree.
suggested_refs: The University of Wooster catalogues for 1911-1913

stops.name: Hillsdale College, Michigan: the degree in English literature
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1915 for the degree (Wikipedia, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman'); month and day default to a June commencement and are not documented. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 41.9203/-84.6303, about 1.4 km south of campus, to the Hillsdale College infobox value.
stops.campa: She finishes at Hillsdale College in Michigan and takes the degree in English literature in 1915, having joined Pi Beta Phi and worked on the college paper. The subject is Shakespeare and the poets. There is no such academic discipline as cryptology anywhere in the United States in 1915, and no place in the country where it is taught to anyone. The same college will award her an honorary doctorate of laws twenty-three years later, or twenty-four: Wikipedia prints 1938 and Hillsdale's own current lists print 1939, and nothing reached here settles it.
suggested_refs: Hillsdale College commencement records, 1915

stops.name: Wabash, Indiana: one school year as substitute principal
stops.date_confidence: attested for the fall of 1915 through the spring of 1916 (Wikipedia, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman'); the day defaults to 01. The specific school building is not identified in any source reached, and the coordinate is Wabash town center.
stops.campa: She takes work as substitute principal at the public high school in Wabash, Indiana, in the fall, and holds it for a single school year: teaching, discipline, the corridor, the register. It is very nearly the whole of what the country offers a woman with a literature degree in 1916, and she does not want it. The building she worked in is not identified in any surviving record, and neither is the reason she gave for leaving. In the spring she goes back to her parents' house, with no position and no prospect.
suggested_refs: Wabash city school records for the 1915-1916 term

segments.name: The Newberry, the Train, and the Baconian Cipher

stops.name: The Newberry Library, Chicago: asking to see the First Folio
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer of 1916 (Wikipedia, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman'); month set to June and day defaulted to 01, neither documented. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 41.9033/-87.6355, about 500 m west of the building, to the Newberry Library at 60 W. Walton St. Her own retelling of the visit comes from interviews given more than fifty years afterward.
stops.campa: In the summer she takes the train up to Chicago and walks into the Newberry Library on West Walton Street to ask whether she may see a copy of the 1623 First Folio, and whether there is any research work to be had in the building. The librarian happens to know a man outside the city who is paying people to hunt a cipher in Shakespeare, and telephones him from the desk. She had come in to ask about a book. The whole scene survives only in interviews she gave more than fifty years afterward, and no contemporary record of the visit has been found.
suggested_refs: The Newberry Library's copy of the 1623 First Folio, 60 W. Walton St., Chicago

stops.name: The train west out of Chicago: what in hell do you know
stops.date_confidence: attested as to the exchange and its setting by her own 1974 interview transcript (Marshall Foundation, 'Tape #5: Fabyan, Riverbank, and the Bilateral Cipher', 6 June 1974, p. 2), which places it on the train out to Geneva, not at the library, and gives Fabyan's line as 'Well, what in hell do you know?'. The pool carried a softened wording and an NSA 1976 attribution; both are corrected here. The date is an ordering device only: no source gives the day.
stops.campa: George Fabyan, a textile millionaire who spends part of his fortune on a private research estate, collects her the same day and puts her on the train out to Geneva, Illinois. He sits down beside her, looks her over, and asks what in hell she knows. She is nonplussed for a moment; then a stubborn streak comes up in her and she looks at him out of her right eye and answers him. He laughs, he roars, loud enough to be heard the length of the car. The train goes on west toward the Fox River. She is twenty-three years old.
stops.quote: That remains, sir, for you to find out.
stops.quote_source: Elizebeth Smith Friedman, recorded interview, Marshall Library, Lexington, Virginia, 6 June 1974, transcript tape 5, p. 2
suggested_refs: Marshall Foundation transcript, 'Tape #5: Fabyan, Riverbank, and the Bilateral Cipher', 6 June 1974
sources: George C. Marshall Foundation, ESF interview transcripts, June 1974

stops.name: Riverbank Laboratories, Geneva: assigned to Mrs. Gallup
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1916 (Wikipedia, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman'); month and day are an ordering device. Coordinate corrected from the pool's 41.8756/-88.3157 to the Fabyan Villa value; Riverbank Laboratories proper is listed at 627 Riverbank Dr., adjacent on the same estate, and the villa coordinate is used throughout rather than a midpoint between the two.
stops.campa: Riverbank is a private estate on the Fox River with laboratories in acoustics, genetics, and codes, all of it funded out of Fabyan's own fortune and answerable to nobody. She is put under Elizabeth Wells Gallup, who believes Francis Bacon hid a biliteral cipher in the typefaces of the early printed Shakespeare and has published at length on it. Elizebeth's assignment is to read the letterforms and record which are italic and which are roman. She does the work honestly for months and cannot get two readers to agree on the same page.
suggested_refs: Elizabeth Wells Gallup, 'The Bi-Literal Cypher of Sir Francis Bacon' (1899)

stops.name: Riverbank, Geneva: the geneticist brought over to the ciphers
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1916 that the two met at Riverbank and that William F. Friedman moved onto the codes and ciphers work (Wikipedia, 'William F. Friedman'); month and day are an ordering device. The photographic collaboration over the Folio pages is the standard account and is not documented in the sources reached here at the level of a specific task order.
stops.campa: Among the estate's staff is William Frederick Friedman, a Russian-born plant geneticist hired to work on wheat, who owns a camera and knows how to photograph and enlarge a printed page. She needs the Folio letterforms magnified; he magnifies them. No document reached here records the task order, only that the two of them worked the pages together and that he courted her over them. The cipher they are working on is not in the book, as she has already begun to suspect. Inside a year he has left genetics entirely for the Department of Codes and Ciphers.
suggested_refs: Riverbank photographic enlargements of the 1623 First Folio typefaces

stops.name: Chicago: the marriage
stops.date_confidence: contested and not resolved. Wikipedia's article on Elizebeth gives May 1917 and Chicago; the photograph caption in the article on William dates the marriage only to 1917. The day, 21 May, is the commonly repeated figure and is not confirmed by any source fetched for this file. No venue is named anywhere reached, so the coordinate is Chicago city center.
stops.campa: They marry in Chicago in May, both of them still on Fabyan's payroll. He is a Russian-born Jew, she is an Indiana Quaker, and the union is also a professional arrangement with no precedent in the country: two working cryptanalysts under one roof, each able to read the other's solutions and each in time holding secrets the other is not cleared to hear. It lasts fifty-two years, until his death. No venue is named in anything reached, and the day, the twenty-first, is repeated everywhere and confirmed nowhere.
suggested_refs: Cook County marriage register, May 1917

segments.name: A Cipher Bureau on a Private Estate

stops.name: Riverbank, Geneva: the country discovers it has no codebreakers
stops.date_confidence: attested that Riverbank functioned as an unofficial cryptologic bureau on United States entry into the war in April 1917, solving intercepted messages and training Army and Navy officers (Wikipedia, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman'). The date given is the declaration of war, used to anchor the stop; the transition was gradual and no single day marks it.
stops.campa: The United States declares war in April and discovers that it has no codebreaking service of any kind. Riverbank, a rich man's hobby estate in Illinois, is the only place in the country where anyone is systematically solving ciphers, so for a season the whole cryptologic capacity of the federal government sits on private ground, under no oversight at all. War, Navy, State, and Justice forward their intercepts out to Geneva. Elizebeth solves them, and teaches Army and Navy officers in classes run on the lawn and in the villa.
suggested_refs: The Riverbank cipher school for Army and Navy officers, 1917-1918

stops.name: Riverbank, Geneva: Publication No. 21
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1918 for Riverbank Publication No. 21, 'Methods for the Reconstruction of Primary Alphabets', credited to William F. Friedman and Elizebeth Smith Friedman jointly. The pool's earlier hedge about the division of authorship is dropped: the joint credit is on the pamphlet. Month and day default to 01-01; the pamphlets are dated by year only.
stops.campa: The Riverbank Publications go out under the laboratory's name, small technical pamphlets that lay the foundation of American cryptanalysis. Number 21, Methods for the Reconstruction of Primary Alphabets, carries both their names, William's and hers. It is a manual for rebuilding an unknown cipher alphabet from the inside, out of the intercepted traffic alone, with no captured key and no machine to help. The method it sets out is the one she will use against rum-runners and against German circuits in South America for the next twenty-five years. The pamphlets are dated by year only; no month is recoverable for any of them. She is twenty-five.
suggested_refs: Riverbank Publication No. 21, 'Methods for the Reconstruction of Primary Alphabets' (Geneva, Illinois, 1918)

stops.name: Riverbank, Geneva: leaving Fabyan
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1921 for the departure to the War Department (Wikipedia, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman': 'In 1921, the Friedmans left Riverbank to work for the United States Department of War'). Month and day default to 01-01. William's 1919 demobilization from the Army, carried in the pool, was not independently confirmed in this pass and is not asserted here.
stops.campa: Fabyan pays them, houses them, and puts the laboratory's name on what they write. In 1921 they leave anyway, for civilian cryptographic work with the War Department in Washington, and the private era of American codebreaking ends with them walking out of it. She is twenty-eight. Behind her are five years spent hunting a cipher that was not in the book, and the discovery, made in the course of failing to find it, that she can do this work. How Fabyan took the departure is not recorded in anything reached: the sources give the year and stop.
suggested_refs: The Fabyan estate at Geneva, Illinois, now a Kane County forest preserve

stops.name: The Munitions Building, Washington: civilian cryptographer
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1921 for the move to Washington and War Department employment (Wikipedia, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman'); month and day are an ordering device. Her specific office is not documented. The coordinate is the Munitions Building on Constitution Avenue near 19th St. NW, corrected from the pool's -77.047, which pinned about 350 m west of it; the building itself is used as an approximation only.
stops.campa: Washington in 1921 is a city of temporary war buildings strung along the Mall, and she goes to work in one of them as a civilian cryptographer for the War Department. Her exact office is not recorded anywhere. What is recorded is the shape of the arrangement she now enters and will not leave for a quarter of a century: federal employment at a woman's salary, work classified the moment it is finished, and a name that appears on nothing the public will read. She and her husband commute in together. The Munitions Building on Constitution Avenue is the likeliest of those buildings, and it stood until 1970.
suggested_refs: The Munitions Building, Constitution Avenue NW, demolished 1970

stops.name: Washington: the resignation, and the Coast Guard's backlog
stops.date_confidence: contested and not resolved. Wikipedia has her quitting the government in 1922, after which the Coast Guard hired her on a temporary basis to clear a backlog; PBS American Experience dates the start of her Coast Guard codebreaking to 1925. The pool's chronology lens anchored the rum-runner work to 1927, which is the date of the Treasury joint unit, an institutional event and not the start of her work. 1925 is used here to order the segment. Barbara born 1923, John Ramsay 1926.
stops.campa: She quits the government in 1922. Barbara is born in 1923 and John Ramsay in 1926, and somewhere in between the Coast Guard comes to her, on a temporary hire, with a backlog it cannot read: the radio traffic of the rum fleet standing off the coast in international water, directing landings by cipher. She takes it. The messages are the ordinary working correspondence of an industry that did not exist before the Volstead Act and will not exist after it. When exactly this begins is contested: Wikipedia puts the hire straight after her resignation, PBS dates her Coast Guard codebreaking to 1925, and nothing reached here settles the two.
stops.quote: Few persons in the present day realize anything of the enormity of the situation in the United States while the Volstead Act, which created the so-called Prohibition Era, was in effect
stops.quote_source: Elizebeth Smith Friedman, 1966 dictated memoir, George C. Marshall Foundation, quoted in The Mob Museum, 'Elizebeth Friedman'
suggested_refs: Elizebeth Smith Friedman, 'History of Work in Cryptanalysis, 1927-1930'

stops.name: Washington: the Treasury's joint unit
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1927 for the joint effort of the Treasury Department's Bureau of Prohibition and Bureau of Customs, and for the arrangement running from 1927 to 1939 folded into the Coast Guard (Wikipedia, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman'). Month and day default to 01-01.
stops.campa: The Bureau of Prohibition and the Bureau of Customs set up a joint effort in 1927, and from that year until 1939 the unit sits inside the Coast Guard with her in it. What she reads is the working correspondence of an industry: ships lying offshore in international water, contact boats running in after dark, shore agents with codebooks and call signs, all of it moving money on a scale the enforcement side cannot come near. She reads it at a desk in Washington, and never sets foot on any vessel she names. The arrangement lasts twelve years.
stops.quote: Never had the criminals found such a gushing well of profits. Never had the anti-criminal forces encountered such universal tidal waves of law breaking.
stops.quote_source: Elizebeth Smith Friedman, 1966 dictated memoir, George C. Marshall Foundation, quoted in The Mob Museum, 'Elizebeth Friedman'
suggested_refs: Records of the Treasury Department cryptanalytic unit, 1927-1939

stops.name: The Pacific coast: teaching Housel the method
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1928 for the trip west to train C. A. Housel, and for Housel's later credit of roughly 3,300 messages over twenty-one months (Wikipedia, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman'); the day defaults to 01. The city is not named in any source reached: San Francisco is used as an approximate Pacific Coast Guard hub and the coordinate carries low confidence.
stops.campa: The traffic is not only Atlantic and Gulf. The Pacific coast has its own fleet and its own systems, and in June she travels west to teach a Coast Guard man named C. A. Housel how the work is done. He will decode some three thousand three hundred messages in the twenty-one months that follow, which is more traffic than she can work herself in that time on top of two other coastlines. The station where she trained him is not named in anything that survives, only the coast.
suggested_refs: Coast Guard intelligence station records, Pacific coast, 1928-1930

stops.name: Washington: the I'm Alone, sunk and then reconstructed
stops.date_confidence: attested for the sinking on 22 March 1929 and for her decryption work supporting the American case in the resulting arbitration (Smithsonian Magazine; her own 'History of Work in Cryptanalysis, 1927-1930'). The stop is pinned in Washington, where she worked, not in the Gulf of Mexico: she was not present at the sinking, and staging her at the scene would be false. The number of messages reconstructed is given as roughly twenty-three in the pool and is not independently confirmed.
stops.campa: On the twenty-second of March the cutters Wolcott and Dexter chase the Canadian schooner I'm Alone into the Gulf of Mexico and sink her, killing a crewman. Canada demands arbitration. The vessel's papers say Canadian ownership, and on paper the United States has shot up a neutral ship. Elizebeth, who is never within a thousand miles of the water, reconstructs the schooner's radio traffic and puts the real owners into the record: an American syndicate flying a flag it had bought. The claims commission reads her decrypts.
suggested_refs: Record of the United States and Canada joint claims commission on the I'm Alone, 1929-1935
sources: Smithsonian Magazine, 'The Coast Guard's Most Potent Weapon During Prohibition'

stops.name: Houston: twenty-four systems in two months
stops.date_confidence: attested for October and November 1929 (Wikipedia, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman'); the day defaults to 01. Corrected from the pool, which gave October alone and described the 650 as messages: the source says 650 smuggling cases subpoenaed by the United States Attorney, in the course of which she decrypted 24 coding systems. The courthouse building at 201 Fannin St. is an approximation and is not confirmed as her working location.
stops.campa: The United States Attorney in Houston has subpoenaed six hundred and fifty smuggling cases and cannot use them, because the evidence is in cipher. She comes down in October and stays through November and reconstructs twenty-four separate coding systems out of the seized traffic alone. No captured keys, no informants, no machine: only the messages, laid against one another until the systems come apart in her hands. Her own account of why they came apart is not a claim about her cleverness.
stops.quote: when choosing a key word, never choose one which is associated with the project with which one is engaged
stops.quote_source: Elizebeth Smith Friedman, 1966 dictated memoir, George C. Marshall Foundation, quoted in 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman and Prohibition', marshallfoundation.org
suggested_refs: The old United States Post Office and Courthouse, 201 Fannin St., Houston
sources: George C. Marshall Foundation, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman and Prohibition'

stops.name: Washington: the memorandum for a unit of seven
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1930 for the memorandum and to the following year for the unit's approval and her appointment as Cryptologist-in-Charge (Wikipedia, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman'); month and day default to 01-01. The figure of roughly 12,000 messages solved by her and one assistant between 1928 and 1930 comes from institutional histories of the Treasury and Coast Guard unit and is not independently verified here.
stops.campa: She writes a memorandum proposing a permanent cryptanalytic organization of seven people, the arrangement to date having been herself and one assistant against every smuggling syndicate on three coasts. Between 1928 and 1930 the two of them are credited with roughly twelve thousand solved messages, a figure that comes from institutional histories and not from any primary count reached here. The government approves the unit the following year and makes her its civilian head, Cryptologist-in-Charge, at thirty-eight, with a staff of men under her.
stops.quote: I must declare with all truth that with one exception, all of the men young or older who have worked for me and under me and with me, have been true colleagues and have never been obstructionists in any way.
stops.quote_source: Elizebeth Smith Friedman, 1966 dictated memoir, George C. Marshall Foundation, quoted in The Mob Museum, 'Elizebeth Friedman'
suggested_refs: Her 1930 memorandum proposing a permanent cryptanalytic unit

stops.name: New Orleans: the Consolidated Exporters trial
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1933 for the New Orleans trial of twenty-three agents of Consolidated Exporters and for her expert testimony (Wikipedia; Smithsonian Magazine names Col. Amos W. Woodcock as lead prosecutor). Month and day default to 01-01. The case-name identification 'United States v. Morrison', carried in the pool, is unverified and is not asserted. The courthouse at 423 Canal St. is a general identification, not confirmed against a trial record. Woodcock's words survive only as reported speech on the Marshall Foundation page, with no underlying document named, so they are not set as a quotation.
stops.campa: Twenty-three agents of Consolidated Exporters, a Vancouver liquor syndicate, stand trial in New Orleans, and the government's case is her decryptions. She takes the stand and explains monoalphabetic substitution to a jury: the frequency of letters in English, the tally laid against the cipher, the technique al-Kindi set down in ninth-century Baghdad that every cryptanalyst since has inherited. Defense counsel cross-examines her for hours. The Marshall Foundation reports that Colonel Amos Woodcock said afterward the case could not have been won without the unit's work and her testimony.
stops.quote: If I remember rightly, this was the only case against smugglers where my work was instrumental in bringing the indictments against Bert Morrison and 22 co-defendants
stops.quote_source: Elizebeth Smith Friedman, 1966 memoir, George C. Marshall Foundation, quoted in The Mob Museum, 'Elizebeth Friedman'
suggested_refs: The old United States Custom House, 423 Canal St., New Orleans
sources: George C. Marshall Foundation, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman and Prohibition'

stops.name: Vancouver: the code groups in Chinese
stops.date_confidence: attested that the Canadian government sought her help in 1937 with an opium-smuggling gang and that she testified in the trial of Gordon Lim and several others (Wikipedia, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman'). Month and day default to 01-01. Four elements carried in the pool remain unverified and are hedged here: the January 1938 conviction date, the RCMP as the requesting body, the arms-trafficking element, and the old Vancouver courthouse at 750 Hornby St. as the trial venue.
stops.campa: The Canadian government asks for her in 1937. A gang running opium is enciphering its traffic through Chinese-language code groups, and she does not read Chinese. She works the structure instead of the words, finding the repetitions, the group boundaries, the shape of the system, and hands the solved skeleton over to translators. She testifies for the Crown at the trial of Gordon Lim and several others. Which Canadian body asked for her is not stated beyond the government itself, and the January 1938 conviction date rests on one unconfirmed lead. Convictions follow, in a courtroom whose identity the surviving accounts do not agree on.
suggested_refs: Canadian Department of Justice and RCMP files on the Gordon Lim prosecution

stops.name: Hillsdale College: the honorary doctorate
stops.date_confidence: contested and not resolved. Wikipedia gives 1938 for the honorary Doctor of Laws from Hillsdale College; Hillsdale's own current institutional lists give 1939. Nothing reached here adjudicates between them. Month and day are an ordering device and are not documented.
stops.campa: Hillsdale calls back the graduate of 1915 and gives her an honorary doctorate of laws. Her current work is classified. Her published output is a handful of technical pamphlets out of a private Illinois laboratory, and the only part of her career the public has been permitted to watch is her testimony in criminal court. Wikipedia dates the award to 1938 and Hillsdale's own current lists to 1939. It is the only degree she will ever hold beyond the bachelor's in English literature she earned on this same campus.
suggested_refs: Hillsdale College honorary degree citations, 1938-1939

stops.name: Washington: the smugglers stop and the circuits do not
stops.date_confidence: reconstruction, and deliberately re-anchored. The pool's chronology lens dated the turn toward German clandestine networks to 1940; PBS American Experience dates her move onto that target to her transfer to the Navy in December 1941, with the South American work running 1942-1944, while Wikipedia ends the Treasury and Coast Guard arrangement in 1939. This stop marks the transition period only, dated 1939 to order the segment, and asserts no single documented event.
stops.campa: Repeal has already taken the rum fleet off the water. What has not stopped is clandestine radio. Through the late thirties her unit keeps working traffic that is no longer about liquor: gun-running, narcotics, and then, as Europe goes to war, transmitters in South America talking to Hamburg in systems that are not commercial codebooks at all. When exactly her target changed is not documented, and the accounts that name a year do not agree on which. The Treasury arrangement runs out in 1939.
suggested_refs: The 1943 'History of OP-20-GU', the unit's own contemporaneous account

stops.name: Walter Reed, Washington: the husband in the neuropsychiatric ward
stops.date_confidence: attested to January 1941 for William F. Friedman's breakdown and hospitalization at Walter Reed, widely attributed to the strain of the work on PURPLE (Wikipedia, 'William F. Friedman'); the pool places the stay at roughly two and a half months, into March. The specific day is an ordering device and is not documented.
stops.campa: William collapses in January under the strain of the work on the Japanese cipher machine the Americans call Purple, and is admitted to the neuropsychiatric section at Walter Reed, where he stays roughly two and a half months. The official cause is anxiety and overwork on secret projects. She keeps the household and the children's routine and says nothing to anyone about where he is, because a cryptologist's breakdown is itself classified, and because she cannot name the machine that caused it. He comes home in March. He goes back to the same work.
suggested_refs: Walter Reed General Hospital, 6900 Georgia Ave. NW, neuropsychiatric section

stops.name: Washington: Unit 387 goes to the Navy
stops.date_confidence: attested for her transfer to the Navy in December 1941 (PBS American Experience) and for her heading Coast Guard Cryptanalytic Unit 387, later folded into Navy communications intelligence as OP-20-GU, working clandestine Latin American radio including intelligence-service Enigma systems in liaison with Intelligence Service Knox at Bletchley Park (Wikipedia, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman'). The day defaults to 01. The Yardley appointment and William Friedman's objection to it are attested in herbert_yardley.journey.json.
stops.campa: With the country at war she goes over to the Navy with her unit, and the Coast Guard's cryptanalytic section becomes OP-20-GU. Her target is the clandestine radio of German intelligence in South America: agents' sets, hand ciphers, and in time several Enigma machines, worked in liaison with Dilly Knox's section at Bletchley Park. Her unit will read four thousand messages on forty-eight circuits before the war ends. Her husband's old antagonist Herbert Yardley is meanwhile hired to run Canada's new unit against the same traffic, over William's stated objection.
stops.quote: Our office doesn't make 'em, we only break 'em
stops.quote_source: NSA Cryptologic Hall of Honor citation for Elizebeth S. Friedman, quoted in Wikipedia, 'Elizebeth Smith Friedman'
suggested_refs: The 1943 'History of OP-20-GU'; Intelligence Service Knox files on Latin American Enigma
sources: herbert_yardley.journey.json, stop 'Ottawa, the Abwehr traffic out of South America'

stops.name: Washington: the Queen Mary reported off Brazil
stops.date_confidence: attested that her unit decrypted German agent traffic reporting the movement of RMS Queen Mary near the Brazilian coast while the ship carried thousands of American servicemen, and that the voyage completed safely (Wikipedia; PBS and Coast Guard accounts). The day defaults to 01. The tradition that her decrypt alone caused a course change saving over 8,000 lives is a later commemorative inference and is not established by any operational record reached; it is stated as tradition in the campa, not as fact.
stops.campa: In March her unit reads German agent traffic out of Brazil reporting the position and course of the Queen Mary, then crossing with thousands of American troops aboard, unescorted, relying on speed alone. The warning goes out. The ship completes her voyage. Whether anything was waiting for her, and whether the warning altered her course, is established by no operational record reached here. The figure of eight thousand lives saved comes from commemorative accounts written long afterward, by people who wanted the story to have a rescue in it.
suggested_refs: Coast Guard and Navy decrypt files on German agent reporting of Allied shipping, 1942

stops.name: Washington: the roundup that burned the source
stops.date_confidence: attested by the unit's own contemporaneous 1943 'History of OP-20-GU', as reported in the pool's dossier, which records that an FBI-directed roundup of German agents in Brazil made premature and overly free use of verbatim decrypts, compromising sources and alerting German controllers to change systems. The day is an ordering device: the history gives the episode to March 1942, not to a date.
stops.campa: The Bureau moves on the German networks in Brazil and makes arrests, quoting decrypted text nearly verbatim as it goes. Berlin reads the arrests correctly, concludes its systems are broken, and changes them. Her unit's own history, written the following year, records the damage in plain language: sources compromised, circuits lost, months of work to be done over from the beginning. That history is not public; what is known of it comes at second hand. She has no authority over the Bureau and no way to stop it.
suggested_refs: The 1943 'History of OP-20-GU', section on the Brazilian roundup
sources: 1943 'History of OP-20-GU' as reported in the research dossier

stops.name: Washington: SARGO, and the traffic out of Buenos Aires
stops.date_confidence: attested that Johannes Siegfried Becker carried the code name SARGO and that the German clandestine networks in South America were later grouped under Operation Bolivar (Wikipedia, 'Operation Bolivar'); month and day are an ordering device for the 1942-1944 span. No source reached places Elizebeth Smith Friedman in Buenos Aires or anywhere in South America: the canonical Buenos Aires pin was deliberately not used as a stop, and the city is named in the campa as the origin of the traffic she read remotely.
stops.campa: The network at the center of it is run out of Argentina by Johannes Siegfried Becker, a German intelligence officer whose radio name is SARGO, and the campaign against it will later be grouped under the name Operation Bolivar. His transmitters talk from Buenos Aires and from safe houses across the continent to receivers in Europe. Everything she knows of Becker's organization arrives as radio traffic at a desk on the Potomac. She never goes to Buenos Aires and never sees one of the sets.

stops.name: Washington: the doll dealer's letters
